steps.tx: **Primary hypothyroidism** has a high TSH and a low free T4. **Subclinical hypothyroidism** has a high TSH and a normal free T4. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the usual cause where iodine intake is sufficient, and **TPO antibodies** support that cause. A single slightly high TSH is repeated before a lifelong label is applied.

vis.alt: Hypothalamic pituitary thyroid axis with a table: primary hypothyroidism has low free T4 and high TSH, central has low free T4 with low or normal TSH, subclinical has normal free T4 and high TSH.
vis.caption: The table matches the laboratory split. Primary hypothyroidism: low free T4 and high TSH. Central hypothyroidism: low free T4 with a low or normal TSH. Subclinical hypothyroidism: normal free T4 and high TSH. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Full replacement **levothyroxine** in a young adult is about 1 point 6 mcg/kg/day, taken fasting and separated from calcium, iron, and some antacids. In older adults and in known coronary disease, start at 25 to 50 mcg and titrate to the **TSH**. A full replacement dose on day one can provoke angina in a patient with coronary disease.

steps.tx: Treat **subclinical hypothyroidism** when the **TSH** is 10 mIU/L or higher. Below that, treat if the patient is pregnant, trying to conceive, or clearly symptomatic, especially if TPO antibodies are positive. A TSH that is only slightly high in an older adult is often watched. Repeat the test before you commit the patient to lifelong replacement.

left.title: Treat
points: TSH at or above 10 mIU/L
Pregnancy or a plan to conceive
Clear symptoms with positive TPO antibodies
A rising TSH on a later sample

right.title: Often watch
points: TSH only slightly high
Older adult without symptoms
No pregnancy plan
Confirm with a second sample first

steps.tx: **Central hypothyroidism** has a low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH. Titrate levothyroxine to the **free T4**, not the TSH, because the TSH cannot be trusted. Replace cortisol first if hypopituitarism is possible. Starting thyroxine while cortisol is missing can precipitate adrenal crisis.

rows: Low free T4, low or normal TSH
Replace cortisol if the pituitary may have failed

steps.tx: **Myxedema coma** is decompensated hypothyroidism with hypothermia, hyponatremia, hypoventilation, and a precipitant such as infection or a sedative. Give intravenous **levothyroxine**, a typical load of 200 to 400 mcg, plus **glucocorticoid** until adrenal insufficiency is excluded. Look for the precipitant. Passive warming is used, and hypoventilation may need support of the airway.

vis.alt: Myxoedema coma diagram with thyroid atrophy, hypothermia, alveolar hypoventilation, sinus bradycardia, pericardial effusion, and a hyponatraemia label.
vis.caption: Decompensated hypothyroidism: thyroid atrophy, severe hypothermia, alveolar hypoventilation, sinus bradycardia, and pericardial effusion. A hyponatraemia label is also present. The drawing is the syndrome, not the intravenous dose. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: In **pregnancy**, increase the **levothyroxine** dose by about 30 percent as soon as conception is suspected, which is two extra tablets a week, and check the TSH about every 4 weeks. Return to the pre-pregnancy dose after delivery. A woman who is already replaced should not wait for the first antenatal visit to take the extra tablets.

rows: About 30 percent more, two extra tablets a week

steps.tx: **Levothyroxine** requirements rise with estrogen, with drugs that induce its metabolism such as **rifampin**, **carbamazepine**, and phenytoin, and with malabsorption or **coeliac disease**. A rising TSH on a stable dose should prompt a review of how and when the tablet is taken, and of new medicines. Calcium and iron taken in the same swallow bind the dose.

left.title: Requirement rises
points: Estrogen, including pregnancy
Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin
Coeliac disease and other malabsorption
Calcium or iron taken with the tablet

right.title: Requirement falls
points: After delivery
After the inducing drug is stopped
After coeliac disease is treated
If the patient loses weight on a full replacement dose

steps.tx: Do not treat **nonthyroidal illness** with **levothyroxine**. A low T3 in a patient in the intensive care unit is an adaptation, not myxedema, unless the history and the free T4 show true hypothyroidism. Reverse T3 is not required to make that distinction on the ward. Repeat the thyroid tests after the acute illness has settled.

left.title: Nonthyroidal illness
points: Low T3 is common in critical illness
It is an adaptation, not myxedema
Levothyroxine is not the treatment
Repeat tests after recovery

right.title: True hypothyroidism
points: History of thyroid disease or neck treatment
Free T4 is low, not only T3
TSH is high if the disease is primary
Replacement is indicated
